title: Serving Voice AI at Scale — Arjun Desai (Cartesia) & Rohit Talluri (AWS)
talk_summary: A fireside chat between Cartesia (a voice-TTS model company) and AWS about serving real-time voice AI, covering latency, SSM architectures, controllability, and edge deployment.

takeaways.technique: Orchestrated pipelines over monolithic models for controllability
takeaways.what_they_do: They argue that composed pipelines (STT + LM + TTS) still beat end-to-end speech-to-speech models in production because each stage is independently controllable and debuggable.
takeaways.evidence_quote: orchestrated solutions are places that you get a lot of controllability around like how you want the different pieces of your system to operate

takeaways.what_they_do: When asked how to distinguish their failures from the customer's, they say evals are essential and that most observed failures actually originate at the LM stage, not the model they sell.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Eval are an incredibly important part of any system that you build.

takeaways.technique: Latency budget slack allocation across stages
takeaways.what_they_do: They deliberately make TTS as fast as possible so the LM stage gets more of the end-to-end latency budget, rather than optimizing every stage equally.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you want to actually give it the most slack
takeaways.numbers: 40 millisecond model latency; 2.5x faster than initial models

takeaways.what_they_do: They run models on-device when network roundtrip plus cloud compute is slower than local inference, citing a 5x speedup for edge over roundtrip.
takeaways.evidence_quote: running our models on edge are about five times faster than if you were to roundtrip
